finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id never enforces authorization: authorize() is called without await, so its 403 is discarded and the report is deleted anyway. Critical.
finding.source: Any HTTP DELETE to /reports/:id by any caller, including one with no session user (req.user is set from req.session.user at server.js:5).
finding.sink: db.reports.remove(report.id) at server.js:21, the protected delete operation.

trace.note: req.user = req.session.user; no check that a user exists
DELETE handler registered with no route-level auth middleware
authorize(...) returns a pending promise with no await; the 403 rejection is unhandled and never reaches the handler
remove runs before grants are checked
authorize body is correct in isolation (throws 403 when 'delete' is not granted), but the throw is never observed

finding.guards_checked: authorize() body (correct in isolation); no await at the call site; no Express error middleware; no route-level auth. The check exists but has no effect on the outcome.
finding.repro: A user with zero grants on report X sends DELETE /reports/X. Expected 403 and no change. Actual: report X is removed and the response is 204. The unhandled 403 rejection also crashes the process on Node >= 15 (default --unhandled-rejections=throw), so the same request is a denial of service. Verified by reading only; the sandbox blocked the stub reproduction, so the crash and deletion ordering are not confirmed by execution.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 does throw a 403 when 'delete' is not granted, but its call at server.js:20 is a bare statement with no await and no try/catch, so the returned promise is never observed. The handler proceeds to db.reports.remove at server.js:21 regardless. No route-level auth middleware (server.js:18) and no error middleware exist in this file. No effective control blocks the delete.
verdict.reason: At server.js:20 authorize(req.user, "delete", report) is called without await, so its async 403 throw (server.js:9-16) becomes an unobserved rejection and server.js:21 runs db.reports.remove(report.id) for any caller who reaches the handler, including one with no grants. Caveats: the file is a fragment (db, req.session, and session middleware are not defined here), so reachability by an anonymous caller depends on session middleware outside this file, and the crash/DoS claim is by reading only, not execution.

finding.claim: An unauthenticated request with a nonexistent report id crashes the process, because the unawaited authorize() and the later report.id access both throw on null. High.
finding.source: DELETE /reports/<nonexistent-id> with no session, or PUT /reports/<nonexistent-id>.
finding.sink: Process-level unhandled promise rejection (Node >= 15 default), which exits the server.

trace.note: db.reports.get returns null/undefined for an unknown id
authorize(req.user, 'delete', null): user.id or resource.id throws; not awaited, so the rejection is unhandled
report.id throws TypeError inside the async handler; Express 4 does not catch async rejections, so this is also unhandled
PUT variant: await authorize(req.user, 'write', null) throws TypeError; the awaited rejection escapes the async handler the same way

finding.guards_checked: No null check on report; no try/catch; no Express 5 async error propagation. The Express version is not pinned in the repo, so this assumes Express 4.
finding.repro: Send DELETE /reports/0 (or PUT) to a running server with no session cookie. Expected 404. Actual: uncaught TypeError and process exit under default Node settings. Verified by reading only; the Node and Express defaults were not executed.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:5 `req.user = req.session.user;` runs on every request before any route. The repo has no session middleware (the only file is server.js), so req.session is undefined and this line throws a synchronous TypeError. Express catches synchronous middleware errors and returns a 500, so the DELETE/PUT handlers at server.js:18-30 are never reached. Also, no package.json pins Express, and under Express 5 async handler rejections go to the error handler instead of crashing.
verdict.reason: As written, every request fails at server.js:5 before reaching the handlers at server.js:18-30, so the claimed null-report crash cannot be triggered; the finding would need a session middleware that is not in the repo, plus Express 4, to hold.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire request body to db.reports.update, so any caller with 'write' on a report can set arbitrary fields, including ownership or id fields. Medium.
finding.source: req.body of PUT /reports/:id, fully attacker-controlled JSON (express.json at server.js:3).
finding.sink: db.reports.update(report.id, req.body) at server.js:28, a persisted write to the report record.

trace.note: express.json() parses any JSON body with no schema
await authorize(..., 'write', report) enforces the write grant only
req.body forwarded unfiltered; no field allowlist

finding.guards_checked: Grant check on 'write' (correct and awaited). No field allowlist or schema validation. The db.update implementation is not in the repo, so whether it filters fields is unknown.
finding.repro: A user with write grant sends PUT with a body containing owner/ownerId, id, or other protected fields. Whether this succeeds depends on the schema behind db.reports.update. Unverified: the db layer is not in this directory.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)` is awaited and throws a 403 on missing grant, so only callers with 'write' on the report reach line 28. No field allowlist or schema validation exists anywhere in server.js; the only guard is the grant check, which does not restrict which fields are written.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (server.js:3 parses any JSON, server.js:27 enforces only the write grant, server.js:28 forwards req.body unfiltered), but whether a write-granted user can actually change ownership or id depends on db.reports.update, which is not in this directory, so the escalation impact cannot be confirmed. Separately, server.js:20 calls `authorize` without `await`, so the DELETE handler at server.js:21 runs without the grant check completing; that is a more serious issue than MASS-1 and should be reported on its own.

finding.claim: Authentication is not enforced in this file: req.user is copied from req.session.user, which is undefined for anonymous callers, and the routes never check it. Medium.
finding.sink: authorize() at server.js:10 dereferences user.id; the protected operations are the routes at server.js:18-30.

trace.note: req.session is undefined in this file (no express-session or cookie middleware is registered), so this line throws on every request; if session middleware is added elsewhere, req.user can be undefined
user.id throws for an undefined user

finding.guards_checked: No authentication middleware, no 401 path, no session middleware in this file.
finding.repro: Not reproducible from this file alone because it is an incomplete fragment. Behavior depends on the session middleware registered in the full app. Unverified.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 (throws 403 when db.grants lacks the action), awaited on the PUT route at server.js:27. The DELETE route's call at server.js:20 is not awaited, so it does not guard anything. Session middleware at server.js:4-7 is not a guard; it copies req.session.user.
verdict.reason: The candidate's trace is wrong: server.js:5 throws (req.session is undefined) rather than yielding an undefined user, and the routes do call authorize (server.js:20, 27), so "routes never check it" is false. The real defect the candidate missed is that the DELETE route calls authorize without await at server.js:20, so the 403 rejection is ignored and server.js:21 deletes the report regardless of the grant check, which is an authorization bypass for any caller, not an authentication gap.
